sections.markdown:
## C2 — Sharing the road continuation and confusables: backing and hill behavior of large vehicles, pilot vehicles, school and other buses, slow and oversize vehicles, funeral processions and stopped vehicles
Continuation facts for the later sharing-the-road pages followed by confusable pairs, each tied to one manual page; knowledge-graph hints (group, difficulty, confusable pair) sit only in the trailing Why it matters line of each block.

FACT_ID: sec06-R01 | anchor: A08
A large vehicle backing up may need to block the street, and you must never cross behind one that is getting ready to back or is already backing. [A08]
Why it matters: group large vehicles; continuation; difficulty easy.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec06-R02 | anchor: A08
Large vehicles lose speed climbing hills and must go slowly downhill to stay in control; smoking wheels or a high speed may mean brake failure, so leave extra space and do not pass. [A08]
Why it matters: group large vehicles; continuation; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec06-R03 | anchor: A08
Pilot vehicles are specially marked cars that lead or follow a vehicle hauling an especially large load. [A08]
Why it matters: group pilot vehicles; continuation; difficulty easy.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec06-R04 | anchor: A08
Meeting an oncoming pilot vehicle, slow down and move as far right as you can while staying in your lane; following one, lengthen your following distance; and pass a pilot vehicle or its load only with caution. [A08]
Why it matters: group pilot vehicles; confusable oncoming versus following; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0062]

FACT_ID: sec06-R05 | anchor: A09
School buses carry flashing amber and red lights high on the front and rear, and some have a stop arm that swings out near the driver's window when the red lights start flashing. [A09]
Why it matters: group school buses; continuation; difficulty easy.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec06-R06 | anchor: A09
Flashing amber lights on a school bus warn that it is about to stop on the road to load or unload children, so get ready to stop. [A09]
Why it matters: group school buses; confusable amber versus red; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec06-R07 | anchor: A09
When a school bus flashes red lights, stop before you reach the bus and stay stopped until the driver switches the red lights off. [A09]
Why it matters: group school buses; confusable amber versus red; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec06-R08 | anchor: A09
On a divided highway whose two roadways are split by an unpaved median strip or a barrier, you stop for a school bus only if you are on the bus's side of the road. [A09]
Why it matters: group school buses; confusable divided highway versus painted median; difficulty hard.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec06-R09 | anchor: A09
A painted median strip or a turn lane does not make two separate roads, so traffic in all lanes must stop for the flashing school bus. [A09]
Why it matters: group school buses; confusable divided highway versus painted median; difficulty hard.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0063]

FACT_ID: sec06-R10 | anchor: A10
Buses serving places of worship and buses carrying workers may use flashing amber and red lights, and you treat those lights exactly as you would on a school bus. [A10]
Why it matters: group other buses; continuation; difficulty medium.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-R11 | anchor: A10
When a transit bus driver signals to pull back into traffic and the electric yield sign on the back of the bus is flashing, vehicles coming from behind must yield. [A10]
Why it matters: group transit buses; continuation; difficulty medium.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-R12 | anchor: A10
Slow moving vehicles such as farm equipment must show the slow moving vehicle emblem on public highways, a fluorescent orange center with a reflective red border, so be ready to slow or change position. [A10]
Why it matters: group slow vehicles; continuation; difficulty easy.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-R13 | anchor: A10
A load sticking out 4 feet or more past the rear of a vehicle must carry a red flag at least 12 inches square at its end. [A10]
Why it matters: group oversize loads; continuation; difficulty hard.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-R14 | anchor: A10
When visibility is limited, the red flag on a rear overhanging load is replaced by a red light that can be seen from 500 feet to the rear and sides. [A10]
Why it matters: group oversize loads; confusable flag versus light; difficulty hard.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-R15 | anchor: A10
A passenger vehicle may carry no load past the left fenders, no more than 6 inches past the right fenders, and no more than 4 feet past the front of the vehicle. [A10]
Why it matters: group oversize loads; confusable left side versus right side limits; difficulty hard.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0064]

FACT_ID: sec06-R16 | anchor: A11
Vehicles in a funeral procession may enter intersections without stopping and need not obey traffic control devices, and other drivers must yield to the procession. [A11]
Why it matters: group funeral processions; continuation; difficulty medium.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec06-R17 | anchor: A11
If you are not part of a funeral procession, joining it or driving between its vehicles is against the law. [A11]
Why it matters: group funeral processions; continuation; difficulty easy.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec06-R18 | anchor: A11
On a road with two or more lanes in your direction, when you approach any stopped motor vehicle showing flashing lights you must change lanes so you are not beside it; the manual also lists slowing to at least 5 miles per hour under the posted limit, and you give the vehicle as much room as is safe. [A11]
Why it matters: group stopped vehicles; continuation; difficulty hard.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec06-R19 | anchor: A11
Near an emergency scene, slow down and be ready to stop, and do not drive over fire hoses unless officials at the scene tell you to. [A11]
Why it matters: group emergency scenes; continuation; difficulty easy.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec06-R20 | anchor: A02
At a signalized intersection you may start your turn once the pedestrian is 6 feet or more from your target lane, but without a signal you wait until the pedestrian has cleared that lane plus the next one. [A02]
Why it matters: group crosswalk turns; confusable signalized versus unsignalized; difficulty hard.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-R21 | anchor: A02
A pedestrian in the lane next to yours requires you to stop and stay stopped, while a pedestrian on the other side of a safety island does not. [A02]
Why it matters: group crosswalks; confusable adjacent lane versus beyond a safety island; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec06-R22 | anchor: A03
The school-hours sign covers set daytime hours on school days only, while the children-present sign applies on any day at any hour children are present. [A03]
Why it matters: group school zones; confusable school-hours sign versus children-present sign; difficulty hard.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec06-R23 | anchor: A06
Following a motorcycle calls for more distance than following a car, and passing a motorcycle calls for giving the rider a full lane. [A06]
Why it matters: group motorcycles; confusable following versus passing; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec06-R24 | anchor: A07
Behind a large vehicle you are in its deep rear blind spot, and beside it you are in a side blind spot unless you can see its driver in the side mirror. [A07]
Why it matters: group large vehicles; confusable rear versus side blind spot; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0061]

corpus_stability.reason: The Oregon Driver Manual is a two-year edition (the front cover names a two-year span and the back cover carries a single form revision code); fees and office details are sent to the DMV website rather than printed, and nothing in the selected pages suggests more than one rewrite per year.
